Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify basic biology and biochemical composition of the meniscus of the knee and labrum of
the shoulder.
Specify the regional variation in the macrostructure and microstructure of the meniscus
attributed to its complex mechanical function.
Determine biomechanical factors to consider for repair and reconstruction of the meniscus.
Meniscus
The knee meniscus is consists of two underlying semilunar, wedge-shaped fibrocartilaginous
tissues between the femoral condyle and the tibial plateau.

The meniscus functions to increase congruity and stability, decrease contact stresses, and
distribute load across the knee joint.
The regional variation in the biochemical components and microstructure of the meniscus is
strongly associated with its complex function.
Development
The menisci arise from a condensation of the intermediate layer of mesenchymal tissue by 8
to 10 weeks of gestation.1
The medial meniscus covers approximately 60% and the lateral meniscus covers 80% of the
corresponding tibial plateau, and this proportion remains consistent throughout
development.2
The vascularity arising from the periphery during development initially extends throughout the
width of the meniscus.
The vascularity of the meniscus gradually decreases to supply only the peripheral 10% to 30%
of the tissue by the time an individual is aged 10 years.2
The cellularity declines, whereas collagen content increases and is organized in a
circumferential fashion during meniscal maturation.2
Anatomy
Gross Anatomy
The knee menisci are wedge-shaped fibrocartilaginous structures situated between the
femoral condyles and the tibial plateau.
The macrostructure of the meniscus is divided into the tibial attachments at the anterior and
posterior roots, the curved anterior and posterior horns, and the meniscal body at its
midportion (Figure 1).
The medial meniscus has a semicircular shape, which covers approximately 50% to 60% of the
medial tibial plateau in adulthood.3
The mean size of the posterior horn in the anterior-posterior dimension is 11 mm, whereas
the anterior horn is narrower.4
The anterior horn of the medial meniscus attaches to the tibia anterior to the anterior cruciate
ligament near the intercondylar fossa with considerable variability.

The transverse, or intermeniscal, ligament connects the anterior horns of the medial and
lateral menisci. The posterior root attachment lies in the posterior intercondylar fossa
between the lateral meniscus and posterior cruciate ligament.5 In addition to its root
attachments, the meniscotibial (coronary) ligament stabilizes the medial meniscus through its
attachment from the inferior aspect of the posterior horn to the tibia.
Peripherally, the medial meniscus is firmly attached to the deep medial collateral ligament and
joint capsule, limiting its mobility.5
The lateral meniscus has a more circular C-shape with symmetric sizes of the anterior and
posterior horns. The lateral meniscus anterior root attaches anterior to the intercondylar
eminence and just lateral to the anterior cruciate ligament insertion site on the tibia, whereas
the posterior root attaches posterior to the lateral tibial spine just anterior to the medial
meniscus posterior root.3
The popliteomeniscal fascicles extend from the lateral meniscus to the posterior capsule to
create the popliteal hiatus. The meniscofemoral ligaments are variably present structures that
connect the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus to the medial femoral condyle. These
ligaments are described by their relationship to the posterior cruciate ligament, with the
ligament of Humphrey crossing anterior to the posterior cruciate ligament and the ligament of
Wrisberg posteriorly.
The less continuous attachment of the lateral meniscus to the capsule allows for greater
meniscal mobility. Several studies have demonstrated this, including Thompson et al,6 which
reported a mean lateral meniscus excursion of 11.2 mm versus a mean medial meniscus
excursion of 5.1 mm occurring from knee extension to flexion.

attachments in relation to the cruciate ligaments of the knee. ACL = anterior cruciate ligament,

LCL = lateral cruciate ligament, MCL = medial collateral ligament, PCL = posterior cruciate
ligament. (Reproduced from Wiley TJ, Tennent DJ, Jayasuriya CT, Twimey-Kozak J, Owens BD:
Meniscus and labrum, in Aaron RK, ed: Orthopaedic Basic Science: Foundations of Clinical
Practice, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 169-180.)
Menisci have three zones that can be discerned based on vasculature and extracellular matrix
composition (Figure 2). These zones are commonly described as white-white, red-white, and
red-red zones (Resource 1).
Figure 2 Illustration shows the meniscal zones. The inner one-third of the meniscus is
avascular and called the white-white zone (WWZ). The middle zone is called the red-white zone
(RWZ) because it has limited vasculature. The outer one-third is called the red-red zone (RRZ)
because it is the most vascularized tissue region that has access to blood supply via vessels
arising from the geniculate arteries. (Reproduced from Wiley TJ, Tennent DJ, Jayasuriya CT,
Twimey-Kozak J, Owens BD: Meniscus and labrum, in Aaron RK, ed: Orthopaedic Basic Science:
Foundations of Clinical Practice, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2021, pp 169-180.)
Neural Anatomy
The posterior articular branch of the tibial nerve innervates the knee along with contributions
from the terminal branches of the obturator and femoral nerves.
In addition, the recurrent peroneal branch of the common peroneal nerve supplies the lateral
portion of the capsule.

Nerve fibers enter the capsule and the peripheral portion of the menisci along a path similar
to that of the blood supply.
The highest nerve density lies in the anterior and posterior meniscal horns, whereas the
peripheral third of the body has greater innervation than the middle third.
Three types of mechanoreceptors have been identified in the human meniscus. Ruffini
endings are type I mechanoreceptors, which have a low threshold and adapt slowly to
pressure and joint deformation. Pacinian corpuscles (type II mechanoreceptors) have a low
threshold but adapt quickly to alterations in tissue tension. Golgi tendon organs (type III
mechanoreceptors) have a high signal threshold and exist in a greater concentration in the
posterior horns, the location at which they play a role in neuromuscular inhibition as the knee
reaches terminal flexion.7
Vascular Anatomy
The blood supply of the menisci arises from the superior, middle, and inferior (medial and
lateral) geniculate arteries as they branch from the popliteal artery.
Synovial artery branches supply the anterior and posterior root attachments, whereas synovial
and capsular artery branches form a perimeniscal capillary network to supply the peripheral
10% to 30% of the meniscus.8
From the anterior and posterior horns, endoligamentous vessels branch into the substance of
the menisci to perform terminal loops and provide direct nutrition over a short distance.9 The
inner one-third of the meniscus is an avascular zone that receives its nutrition from the
synovial fluid via loading diffusion.10
Composition and Structure
The human meniscus is a well-organized structure consisting of fibrochondrocytes dispersed
among a dense extracellular matrix.
The predominant meniscal cells, serving to produce and maintain the extracellular matrix, are
frequently referred to as fibrochondrocytes.
However, fibrochondrocytes often is considered an inconclusive or controversial term given
the limited experimental evidence proving that these cells produce fibroblast markers and
chondrocytes.
Some literature suggests meniscal cells are likely a mixture of fibroblasts and chondrocytes.
Conversely, a recent study demonstrated that mesenchymal stem cells can differentiate

fibrochondrocytes that simultaneously produce type I and type II collagen.11
The fibrochondrocytes in the superficial layer of the meniscus appear flattened with their
fusiform shape, whereas those in the deeper portion of the meniscus are regionally variant.
Red-red zone cells display many processes, red-white zone cells display some cell process, and
white-white zone cells are rounded and chondrocyte-like11 (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Illustrations show the cell types of the meniscus, distribution, and morphology.
Superficial zone cells are flattened (A), red-red zone cells display many cell processes (B), red-
white zone cells display some cell processes (C), and white-white zone cells are rounded and
chondrocyte-like (D).
Consistently, meniscus cells from the inner white-white zone readily produce type II collagen
and proteoglycan compared with cells from the outer red-red zone,12 supporting the regional
heterogeneity of meniscal cell phenotype.
In the extracellular matrix of the meniscus, water accounts for 65% to 75% of the overall
weight and volume.3
Composing 75% of the dry weight, collagens are the predominant extracellular matrix
component and provide tensile strength to the meniscus.13

Type I collagen comprises most of this collagen content, with small contributions of collagen
types II, III, V, and VI.14
The most superficial layer has randomly oriented collagen fiber, whereas type I collagen fibers
are organized circumferentially within the meniscus parallel to its peripheral border (Figure 4).
The circumferentially oriented fibers are bound together by interspersed radially oriented tie
fibers providing structural support.3
Matrix proteins other than collagen account for 8% to 13% of the meniscal dry weight.3
Fibronectin is a matrix protein involved in cellular processes such as cell migration/adhesion
and tissue repair, whereas elastin likely contributes to tissue resiliency.14
Proteoglycans are large, negatively charged molecules consisting of one or more
glycosaminoglycan side chains covalently bonded to a core protein. These hydrophilic
molecules exist within the extracellular matrix and contribute to 1% to 2% of the dry weight.
The primary type in the meniscus is aggrecan, followed by decorin, biglycan, and
fibromodulin.15
Proteoglycans play an important role in the hydration of meniscal tissue and its viscoelastic
ability to resist compressive forces.
The meniscal horns and the inner 50% of the weight-bearing meniscus contain the highest
concentration of glycosaminoglycan side chains.16
The most common glycosaminoglycans in the adult meniscus include chondroitin-6-sulfate
(40%), chondroitin-4-sulfate (10% to 20%), dermatan sulfate (20% to 30%), and keratan sulfate
(15%).13,17
Consistent with the regional variance in cell phenotypes, cartilaginous matrices, such as
proteoglycan and type II collagen, are predominantly present in the white-white zone rather
than the red-red zone.

Figure 4 Illustration shows the collagen architecture of the knee meniscus. From core to
surface, the collagen arrangement changes from structured to unstructured. Three main types
of collagen orientations are present in the meniscus: circumferential, radial, and random.
Circumferential fibers are the most abundant in the tissue and are found in the deep zone.
Radial fibers are dispersed throughout the deep zone and are present on the periphery and at
the horns of the meniscus in the lamellar zone. Despite the presence of radial fibers, random
fiber orientation dominates the lamellar zone. In the superficial zone, fiber orientation typically
is random in the superior region and more radially oriented in the inferior region.
Biomechanics
The knee meniscus is estimated to bear 45% to 75% of the total joint load, varying with the
degree of joint flexion, animal model, and tissue health.18
If the meniscus is removed, the support of the femoral condyles is drastically reduced and the
joint force is concentrated on the hyaline cartilages, increasing stress on the tissue to two to
three times higher than normal.19
The regionally variant collagen orientation in the meniscus is suitable for its complex
mechanical functions.
The random collagen fiber orientation in the most superficial layer of the meniscus provides
tensile strength and resistance to shear forces.

Circumferentially oriented collagen fibers in the deep meniscus allow for conversion of
vertically oriented compressive forces into circumferential hoop stresses distributed
throughout the meniscus.15
The tensile modulus of the meniscus is approximately 100 to 300 MPa in the circumferential
direction, which is 10 times higher than in the radial direction.
Tensile properties in the circumferential direction are considerably higher than in the radial
direction given the predominant circumferential fibers with the small portion of radial tie
fibers.
Under compression, the aggregate modulus of the meniscus is 100 to 150 kPa.
In shear, the tissue exhibits a shear modulus of approximately 120 kPa.
The tensile and compressive moduli also vary in different anatomic locations (eg, inner and
outer; anterior, central, and posterior).
The regional and directional complexity of the biomechanical properties of the meniscus has
been a roadblock in development of a bioengineered, functional meniscal graft.
Labrum
The labrum is a fibrocartilaginous tissue that supports congruency and stability of the shoulder
joint.
The labrum is a rim-like structure attached around the margin of the glenoid cavity that
increases the contact area of the humeral head and the scapula and supports load
distribution.
Development
During normal fetal development, the superior glenoid labrum begins to coalesce with the
biceps tendon by approximately 9 weeks of gestation.
Additional anterior and posterior consolidations appear and transition to a highly vascular,
primitive fibrocartilaginous structure with distinct transitions from the glenoid to the labrum
from approximately 12 to 20 weeks of gestation.20,21
However, mature labral tissue is not present until a fetus full term, with a gradual transition to
mature fibrocartilage during the first several years of life.21,22
Throughout life, an increased proportion of elastin and decreased vascularity correlate with
increasing age.21

Composition and Structure
The glenoid labrum is primarily composed of type II collagen and aggrecan, which may help
provide joint lubrication and fluid motion.23,24
However, after injury, animal studies have shown increased levels of interleukin-1 beta,
transforming growth factor beta-1, and matrix metalloproteinases-3 and -13 inflammatory
cytokines, as well as increased proportions of type III collagen consistent with
fibrocartilaginous scar formation.25
The microstructure of the labrum can be divided into three layers. The superficial layer is
composed of a thin, woven, mesh-like matrix that has been proposed to absorb compressive
forces across the labrum while assisting with joint lubrication and proteoglycan storage.23
The second, or intermediate, layer consists of multidirectional fibrillar bundles arranged
parallel to the glenoid rim and acts to resist various stresses and force vectors.23
The deepest layer of the labrum is composed primarily of a dense core of circumferential
fibers that likely help disperse hoop stresses and tensile forces resulting from glenohumeral
joint compression and humeral head translation.23
The labral attachment to bone consists of a cellular region of vertical and oblique interwoven
collagen and fibers that insert into the superficial bone and the hyaline cartilage via Sharpey
fibers that resist multidirectional stresses.23
The capsulolabral soft-tissue footprint on the glenoid articular surface and neck is most
prominent in the anterior/inferior region of the glenoid and ranges between 8.4 and 9.4 mm in
width.26,27
Anatomic studies have shown that double-row Bankart repair re-creates considerably more
(85.9% versus 42.3%) of this native glenoid labral attachment compared with single-row
repair.26
However, biomechanical and clinical studies have not yet shown the clinical superiority of
double-row labral repair compared with the more commonly performed single-row repair.28
Underlying the capsulolabral footprint, the labral insertion on the glenoid has a relatively
avascular 7-mm-wide calcified fibrocartilaginous footprint that allows for direct attachment of
the soft tissue to the glenoid.29 This calcified fibrocartilage is relatively avascular compared
with the adjacent glenoid bone.
In addition, the labrum overlies the glenoid articular surface between 2.5 and 4.6 mm.29,30
Therefore, appropriate glenoid rim débridement and anchor placement on the peripheral 2 to
3 mm of the glenoid face may allow for more anatomic reconstruction during Bankart repair

for glenohumeral instability and should routinely be performed to allow for optimal healing

This fibrocartilaginous footprint also is an anatomic justification for double-row labral repair.
Biomechanical studies assessing the native footprint have shown a more anatomic restoration
of the native labral footprint on the glenoid, an increased ultimate load to failure, and less
total displacement of the osseous fragment during bony Bankart repair than during standard
single-row labral repair.31
However, clinical studies have not yet shown any relevant effect on clinical or functional
patient outcomes.31
Vascular Supply
The labrum has a high propensity to heal because of its robust vascular supply.
The superior and anterosuperior labrum is supplied from branches of the ascending glenoid
artery, suprascapular artery, and circumflex scapular artery, as well as the muscular branches
of the subscapularis.
The anterior-inferior Bankart region is supplied from the circumflex scapular artery, posterior
circumflex humeral artery, and circumflex scapular artery, as well as the muscular branches of
the triceps and subscapularis.
The posterior labrum is supplied from branches of the suprascapular artery and muscular
branches of the teres minor and infraspinatus.32
The importance of this blood supply may partially account for the excellent outcomes after
properly performed labral surgery with appropriate osseous preparation.
Neural Anatomy
The glenoid labrum contains free sensory nerve fibers consistent with the pain response
associated with labral pathology and encapsulated nerve fibers that likely play a role in
glenohumeral proprioception.33
The most common sensory nerve endings in the labrum are Ruffini corpuscles, which are slow
adapting and responsive to prolonged stimuli, such as stretching and compression.34
These nerve endings are similar to those in the knee and resemble those in the meniscus and
the anterior cruciate ligament.
The labrum also contains fewer type II mechanoreceptors, which are fast adapting and
responsive at the ends of motion. They are primarily located superficially at the glenolabral

Biomechanics
The glenoid labrum has several functions, with the primary goal of providing a static constraint
to the glenohumeral joint.
The macroscopic structure of the labrum allows it to reduce humeral head translation on the
glenoid by as much as 20% compared with shoulders in which labral resection was performed
by providing a static block to motion with humeral head compression.35,36
The labrum partially accomplishes this role by increasing the relative depth of the native
glenoid in the anterior-posterior and superior-inferior dimensions, thereby allowing a more
stable structural constraint than the glenoid in isolation.35,36
The labrum also improves stability by increasing the total contact area of the glenohumeral
joint. This allows for increased glenohumeral stability by increasing the dynamic stable range
of motion.
The labrum accomplishes this by increasing the surface area by which the glenoid articulates
with the humeral head despite their different radii of curvature.37 This ultimately allows for
increased functional range of motion.
Similarly, analogous to the knee meniscus, the labrum helps disperse contact pressures across
the glenohumeral joint by increasing the total surface area by which the glenoid articulates
with the humeral head.35,36
This function is evident in its microscopic structure that effectively dissipates hoop stresses
and in studies indicating that an incompetent labrum leads to increased glenoid contact
pressures and joint overloading.23,38
In addition, these pressures have been shown to decrease to their baseline, even in patients
with glenoid bone loss of less than 20%, after labral repair.38
The labrum also helps increase glenohumeral stability by creating a negative intra-articular
pressure seal that prevents glenohumeral dissociation during traction and distraction
events.39
The effect is most apparent after disruption of the labral seal, the location at which increased
humeral translation in all directions is evident.39,40
